idiom_name: java.rmi stub (forwarder) + exported remote object (receiver) over object serialisation
implementation_notes: RMI is this pattern built into the JDK: a remote interface implemented on the server is exported, and the client holds a stub whose method call marshals the arguments and ships them over the connection (the forwarder), while the server unmarshals, resolves the target object and invokes the method (the receiver); the RMI registry behind Naming.lookup is the name-to-address map, and MarshalException/UnmarshalException mark the marshalling boundary. Modern JDKs fold the old server-side skeleton into the runtime, and Java object serialisation of untrusted data is explicitly warned against, so new peers usually keep the shape (interface plus stub) and swap the mechanism for gRPC/Netty or a hand-rolled frame codec over java.nio. The classic RMI structure is still the shortest path for two JVMs on a trusted network that already share the same classes.
pitfalls: RMI passes Serializable objects by copy but Remote objects by reference, so adding a Remote parameter silently turns a local call back into a network call.
serialVersionUID must be pinned, or any class edit makes peers fail to unmarshal each other (InvalidClassException).

Deserialising an untrusted stream is a code-execution surface - use serialization filters or a safer codec - and a dropped connection only surfaces at the next call as UnmarshalException/ConnectIOException.
